progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b07: UV damages DNA in skin cells and mutations can build up over decades (latency); exposure raises risk, not certainty; SunSmart's five actions; population exposure reduction lowers disease. From b10: rates compare groups fairly; incidence counts new cases. From b11: control group, confounder, dose-response, self-report as a limitation, the benefit chain (finding, decision, action, outcome checked). From b12: type 2 diabetes is driven by insulin resistance linked to excess body fat and low activity (attempt 10c only). Not assumed: prevention (as a defined term), primary, secondary and tertiary prevention, campaign, upstream, process, impact and outcome measures, secondary source, attribution, equity.
progression.startsWith: Australia has one of the highest melanoma rates in the world. In 1981, a Victorian campaign told people to slip, slop, slap, and in 1988 it grew into SunSmart. Today, melanoma rates in younger Australians are falling. But was that the campaign, or something else? So how can prevention campaigns reduce disease, and how do we know one worked?
progression.stopsAfter: defining prevention and naming primary, secondary and tertiary prevention with an example of each; defining a campaign; designing from the mechanism (exposure, audience, action, measure); explaining why knowledge alone rarely changes behaviour and why changing conditions works better; distinguishing process, impact and outcome measures and matching them to time; evaluating SunSmart with impact evidence (more hats, sunscreen and shade, less sunburn; more advertising, less sunburn) and outcome evidence (falling melanoma in younger Australians, rising in older Australians, explained by latency); judging the secondary sources and the attribution (no control group, self-report, other changes; a package, not the ads alone); explaining equity and proposing an improvement that targets the highest-risk groups and measures them separately; applying this to an unseen school campaign and to an unseen type 2 diabetes campaign.
progression.nextLesson: when genetics can help prevent disease (bio-m8-b14).

teaching.task: In 1981, a campaign told Australians to slip, slop, slap. Today, melanoma rates in younger Australians are falling. How can prevention campaigns reduce disease, and how do we know one worked?
teaching.causalExplanation: You've seen how UV damages DNA in skin cells. Prevention means acting before disease or harm develops. Primary prevention stops the exposure itself, like sun protection. Secondary prevention catches disease early, before symptoms, like screening. Tertiary prevention limits the damage once disease is established. A campaign is a planned program of messages and actions, aimed at a defined group, to change one behaviour. Good campaigns start from the mechanism. For melanoma, the risk is UV reaching skin cells, so the target behaviour is reducing that exposure, especially in childhood, when sunburn adds the most risk. Then choose the audience, and decide before you start what you'll measure. If you can't name the exposure, the people and the measure, it's an advert, not a strategy. Here's the problem campaigns run into. People learn the message, agree with it, and still don't change, because habit, cost, convenience and what others do matter more than information. So SunSmart didn't rely on ads. Schools adopted hat and shade policies, councils built shade, UV alerts went into weather forecasts, and commercial solariums were banned. These change the conditions, so the safe choice becomes the easy one. Tobacco control worked the same way, with taxes and smoke-free laws alongside the ads.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Australia has one of the highest melanoma rates in the world. You've seen how UV damages DNA in skin cells. Good campaigns start from the mechanism. Here's the problem campaigns run into. So how do you measure whether it worked? Process measures count what the campaign did: ads shown, schools signed up. SunSmart has impact evidence over thirty years. Now outcomes. So how sure can we be? Judge the secondary sources first, data someone else collected: who produced them, when, is there real data, and do independent sources agree? Here, they're health agencies and peer-reviewed studies that agree. Effectiveness also means equity: whether the benefit reaches the people at highest risk. Two exam questions. Shade and a uniform hat protect students without relying on memory. Second. Change the conditions, not just the message. So, for any campaign.
teaching.openingDecision: Australia has one of the highest melanoma rates in the world. In 1981, a Victorian campaign told people to slip, slop, slap, and in 1988 it grew into SunSmart. Today, melanoma rates in younger Australians are falling. But was that the campaign, or something else? So how can prevention campaigns reduce disease, and how do we know one worked?
teaching.understandingCheck: Two exam questions. First. A school built shade sails and added broad-brimmed hats to its uniform. Over one school year, independent observers counted more students in shade at lunch, and UV meters worn by some students recorded 40 per cent less exposure. Evaluate this strategy for preventing melanoma. Pause here to answer. Second. A council ran an online campaign about type 2 diabetes. Afterwards, residents knew more about its risk factors, but physical activity didn't change. Many residents work long shifts, and few streets have footpaths. Propose two changes that would make the strategy more effective, and a way to measure its success. Pause here to answer.
teaching.curriculumScope: B8-IQ4-01: "use secondary sources to evaluate the effectiveness of current disease-prevention methods and develop strategies for the prevention of a non-infectious disease, including but not limited to:" with the listed example "educational programs and campaigns" (this video; "genetic engineering" is b14's). Evaluate effectiveness: scenes 5 to 8, attempt 10a. Use secondary sources: scene 8. Develop strategies: scenes 3, 4 and 9, attempt 10c. Inquiry question: "How can non-infectious diseases be prevented?" (answered in part; b14 completes it).

design.visualSystem: One campaign board. A coded campaign frame owns the bottom fifth of the frame from scene 3 to scene 9: four slots, "exposure", "audience", "action", "measure" (b07's PathwayStrip, four-slot mode), filled for SunSmart in scenes 3 and 4. From scene 5, a coded evidence ladder stands at the right: three rungs, bottom to top, "process: what we did", "impact: what people did", "outcome: what the disease did", each rung lighting when its evidence is shown, with a small time bar beside it ("months", "years", "decades"). Above the frame, one painted plate or a coded chart at a time. Data are coded charts only (house bar chart, coded lineGraph). No people, hands or faces: behaviour is shown by objects (hat and sunscreen, shade sail, work shirt and hat), surveys by the clipboard plate, groups by coded dot rows. No campaign logos, mascots or brand marks; campaign names appear as plain text chips. At most three bright text items at once; earlier labels dim to grey.

scenes.visualReference: the board clears. The card writes on, tagged "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience". Stem: "A school built shade sails over its playground and made a broad-brimmed hat part of its uniform. Over one school year, independent observers recorded more students in shade at lunchtime, and personal UV meters worn by a sample of students recorded 40% less UV exposure during school hours than in the year before." Demand: "Evaluate the effectiveness of this policy as a strategy for preventing melanoma. (5 marks)". m8-shade-sail-v1.png (this lesson's plate) sits small at the card's upper left; no other plate. The countdown ring starts after "Pause here to answer." and runs for 10 seconds. The whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it.

On "without relying on memory" "built shade sails" and "part of its uniform" underline (tag "conditions, not information"). On "classic mistake" a chip "melanoma has been prevented" writes and takes a grey scribble cross, small text "impact now, outcome later". Settle one second.

scenes.visualReference: the board clears. The card writes on, tagged "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience". Stem: "A local council ran a six-month online campaign about type 2 diabetes. A survey afterwards showed residents knew more about its risk factors, but measured physical activity did not change. Many residents work long or irregular shifts, and few streets in the area have footpaths." Demand: "Propose TWO changes that would make this prevention strategy more effective, and a way to measure its success. Justify each part. (5 marks)". m8-walking-shoes-v1.png (b12) sits small at the card's upper left. The countdown ring starts after "Pause here to answer." and runs for 10 seconds. The whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it.
